subject: religious-studies
title: Utilitarianism: Bentham and Mill
welcome_lead: Enter the workshop of nineteenth-century reform where Jeremy Bentham and John Stuart Mill argued that the good is the greatest happiness of the greatest number.
meta_desc: A-Level AQA Religious Studies adventure on classical utilitarianism, the hedonic calculus, Mill's qualitative pleasures, and act versus rule utilitarianism.
final_note: You have followed the consequentialist thread from Bentham's calculus to Mill's higher pleasures.

concepts.def: Actions are right insofar as they tend to promote happiness, wrong insofar as they produce its reverse.
Bentham's seven criteria for measuring pleasure: intensity, duration, certainty, propinquity, fecundity, purity, extent.
Each individual act is judged by the utility it produces in that situation.
Rules are adopted because following them generally maximises utility; associated with Mill.
Mill's intellectual and moral pleasures, qualitatively superior to bodily 'lower' pleasures.
Mill's principle (in On Liberty) that the only legitimate ground for coercion is preventing harm to others.

walkthroughs.body_html: In An Introduction to the Principles of Morals and Legislation (1789), Bentham declares that 'nature has placed mankind under two sovereign masters, pain and pleasure'. The hedonic calculus weighs intensity, duration, certainty, propinquity (nearness), fecundity (likelihood of more pleasure), purity (freedom from pain) and extent (number of persons affected). This is a strictly quantitative hedonism.

Mill, in Utilitarianism (1863), insisted that pleasures differ in quality, not just quantity. 'It is better to be a human being dissatisfied than a pig satisfied; better to be Socrates dissatisfied than a fool satisfied.' Competent judges who have experienced both will prefer the higher pleasure, which gives Mill a way to dodge the 'doctrine worthy only of swine' objection.

Act utilitarianism risks justifying horrors (the sheriff who hangs an innocent man to prevent a riot). Rule utilitarianism replies that a rule against punishing the innocent yields more utility long-term. Critics like Bernard Williams argue rule utilitarianism collapses into act utilitarianism whenever breaking the rule would maximise utility (the 'rule worship' charge).
